title: the Beatles and the mantra
hook: a harmonium, a drum, one voice, and a whole room singing it back
tomorrow: who are the singers with a drum on the city sidewalk?

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Beatles and the mantra, Narada asked Brahma for the chant's rules and heard there were none. Today, the last part: the names sung together.
screen: `NO RULES OF TIME, PLACE OR PURITY.`

segments.voice: A student hall on a Friday night, chairs pushed to the walls. Someone pumps a harmonium and it wheezes into a chord. A drum picks up the beat. One voice sings a short line of names, and the room sings it back, a little ragged. Then again, a little faster. At the back, a first-timer who swears she can't sing is reading the words off a friend's lips. A few rounds in, her mouth is moving. Soon, nobody in the room is the audience. How did that happen?
screen: `A HARMONIUM WHEEZES INTO A CHORD.` → `ONE VOICE, THEN THE ROOM.` → `NOBODY IS THE AUDIENCE.`

segments.voice: That's kirtan: singing God's names and glories, often in call and response. Last week went quiet with the silent mantra; kirtan is the loud end of the same practice. The Bhagavata Purana gives it a special place. In the age of Kali, it says, the wise worship the Lord through sankirtana, singing his names together. Not a sacrifice only priests can perform. A song anyone can join, even the one at the back. The same Purana pictures Narada, the sage who asked for the chant's rules, wandering the worlds with his vina, singing of God as he goes. A traveling singer, carrying the names from place to place. That's a useful picture for the Beatles' part in this story too. A pop song with a chant in its chorus is not a kirtan. But it carried the sound of one into rooms that had never heard it. A band went looking for a silent word, and a chant to sing out loud traveled home with them. Both ends of the practice made the trip. And somebody would soon take the singing out onto the street.
screen: `KIRTAN: THE NAMES, CALLED AND ANSWERED.` · `SANKIRTANA: THE WORSHIP OF THE WISE.` · `NARADA AND HIS VINA.` · `BOTH ENDS MADE THE TRIP.` · then, large: `THE ROOM ANSWERS THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sing or hum one short line softly: a name you hold dear, or simply a note. Then pause, as if a room were singing it back, and let the pause be as full as the line. Keep that rhythm, call and quiet answer, until the breath settles into it.
The Beatles and the mantra: from a silent word in Rishikesh to names sung together in kirtan, the last stop on this road.
screen: `THE BEATLES AND THE MANTRA — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road, from the Beatles and the mantra: in kirtan, the room answers the voice. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1716 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO ARE THE SIDEWALK SINGERS?`

fork.setup: at a family puja, your uncle leads a bhajan and your teenage cousins stand at the back with their phones, 'just watching.' what would make it kirtan?
options: everyone answering the line, even softly, so no one is just watching.
a better speaker, so the leader's voice reaches the back of the room.
a trained singer up front, so the music sounds the way it should.
fork.reveal: kirtan is call and response: one voice sings the names, and the room sings them back. the Bhagavata calls singing them together the worship of the wise.

original.note: Sanskrit kirtana, singing God's names and glories; sankirtana is singing them together.
